questions.q: Why is a hardening project that only exists in Mara's head and terminal history not actually finished?
options: Because Dale requires a PDF for every project regardless of content
Because none of that knowledge is usable by anyone else at Hartwell if Mara is out, which makes the whole effort a single point of failure
Because unwritten configuration automatically reverts after 30 days
Because CIS Benchmarks require a notarized document
questions.explain: Writing the baseline down is what turns a one-time favor into something the rest of the team can actually rely on and repeat without Mara personally present.

questions.q: What are the five sections of each runbook entry in this lesson's format?
options: Title, author, date, version, signature
What it is, why it matters, how to apply it, how to verify it, and owner/review cadence
Scope, baseline, detection target, deliverable, timeline
Summary, risk score, CVE reference, patch level, vendor contact
questions.explain: Each checklist item is documented with what it is, why it matters, exactly how to apply it, exactly how to verify it, and who owns re-checking it over time.

questions.q: Why does the Sentinel rule's documentation need to include the Lesson 6 test scenarios, not just the finished KQL query?
options: Sentinel requires test scenarios to be stored alongside every rule
So a future analyst editing the query has a ready-made regression test to re-run and confirm the rule still behaves correctly
Because the query won't run without the test scenarios present
Because the test scenarios replace the need for entity mapping
questions.explain: Documenting the expected true-positive and false-positive outcomes gives anyone who edits the query later a concrete way to check they haven't broken its logic.

questions.q: What is the difference between the runbook and the changelog in this lesson?
options: They are two names for the same document
The runbook describes the current state of the baseline; the changelog records what changed and when, chronologically
The changelog is only used for the Sentinel rule, never for server hardening
The runbook is written by Dale; the changelog is written by Mara
questions.explain: The runbook answers "what's true right now"; the changelog answers "how did it get this way" — conflating them makes each harder to use for its actual purpose.

questions.q: In the sample SSH runbook entry, what does the "Verify" line specifically provide that the "How" line does not?
options: A list of every server at Hartwell
A concrete command/check confirming the setting actually took effect, rather than just describing how to configure it
The owner's contact information
A history of every previous SSH configuration
questions.explain: "How" documents the configuration step; "Verify" documents the proof that it actually applied — the same configured-vs-confirmed distinction from Lessons 3 and 4.
